k-1.x_notes: Strong, concrete sequence of ten problems over five pages, all built on drawn counters: choosing first/second for small {1,2} piles, crossing out the winning move (4,5,7,8), classifying piles 1-12, beating greedy Ben (answers 3,4,6,7, a nice twist since 6 is beatable against a greedy player), rule changes {1,2,3} and {1,3}, a 20-counter comparison across rules, two-pile pairs (2,2 / 1,2 / 3,3 / 1,4 all correct), and enumerating every game from 4 and 5 counters (5 and 8 ways). Enough work for the whole time, no cutesy text. Weaknesses: the two-pile Problem 8 relies on the shared rule 'whoever takes the last counter wins', which a kindergartner can easily read as emptying one pile; 'Color' requires crayons that are not on the materials list; ring-drawing rows in P9/P10 are tighter (though they give two spare rows). Footer lacks an id, same as Y.
k-1.y_notes: Essentially the same packet, with the same strengths and correct answers throughout. Differences: Problem 8 adds 'Whoever takes the very last counter wins', which removes the main ambiguity in the two-pile game; it uses 'Circle' consistently, so only pencils are needed; the P9/P10 counter grids are more widely spaced, which makes drawing rings easier for small hands, but they have only one spare row each (6 rows for 5 games, 9 for 8). Footer lacks an id, same as X.
k-1.reason: The packets are nearly identical; Y's explicit last-counter rule for the two-pile game prevents a likely K-1 misunderstanding, and its roomier ring grids are easier to use.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Excellent and correct development: play {1,2} piles, test four claimed strategies (Mia wins, Leo loses e.g. 10-8-6-4-3-1-0, Ana wins, Sam always loses because 10 is not a multiple of 3), classify 1-20 under {1,3,4} (second at 2,7,9,14,16), extend to 25/30/37/50 (1st, 2nd, 2nd, 1st), test greedy Kai (loses), mirroring Theo (loses), and Zoe's correct 7-or-2 plan (wins against every reply), then Jon's claim about {1,2,4} vs {1,2} (identical, so Jon is wrong) and two-pile pairs (5,5 / 3,6 / 2,5 second, 1,5 first). Matches the outline's emphasis on testing strategies against every reply. Weakness: Problem 6 never says what to write in the 1-15 table and gives no space to answer 'Is Jon right?', so children will have to ask; the shared rules carry a slightly redundant clause.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Same problems and same correct mathematics. Problem 6 says to put an X under each pile where you would rather go second and gives an answer box, so the table and the question are usable without asking. Problem 5 adds a request to explain why a winning plan (Zoe's) wins against every reply, which is the central kernel for this band rather than a routine add-on. Otherwise identical layout and workspace.
grades-2-3.reason: Same strong content, but Y's Problem 6 tells children what to record and gives space for the answer, and its Problem 5 asks them to justify the winning plan, which directly serves the band's goal.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Rich, correct nine-problem sequence: {1,2} table and 100 counters, {1,3,4} W/L to 30 with the period-7 pattern, seven rules with three matching pairs ({1,2}/{1,2,4}, {1,3}/{1,3,5}, {1,4}/{1,4,6}), greedy Kai (fails at 5,8,10,...; works only for {1,3} and {1,3,5}), inverse problems, two-pile grids, Grundy values for {1,3,4} (11&13 losing, 12&18 winning), and {1,6,9}, which becomes periodic with period 5 only from 10 on, a good illustration of 'eventually'. Weakness: in Problem 5 the first two lists (4,8,12,... and 2,5,7,10,12,15,...) are exactly the {1,2,3} and {1,4} rows already completed in Problem 3, so half of the inverse problem is a look-up. Problem 7 is a bare grid fill with no question and no answer space. Small cells in Problem 3 are awkward to circle.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same sequence and correct mathematics, with a better Problem 5: 5,10,15,... (generalize to {1,2,3,4}) and 2,8,10,16,18,... (needs construction, e.g. {1,4,5}), followed by the shared 0,3 mod 7 case ({1,2,6}) and the impossible 0,3 mod 5 case. This gives a real build-up from easy to constructive to impossible. Problem 7 asks which pairs are losing and gives a box, which sets up the Grundy labels in Problem 8. Problem 4 asks children to explain one greedy-works case. 'Shade' suits the small cells in Problem 3.
grades-4-5.reason: Y's inverse-problem lists all need new thinking, while two of X's four are already answered in Problem 3, and Y's Problem 7 has a purpose and space instead of being a bare grid fill.

overall.reason: The two packets share the same well-designed, mathematically correct problems, so the choice rests on small but consistent differences. Y is at least as good in every band: it clarifies the two-pile rule for K-1, tells 2-3 children what to record and gives them space in Problem 6, and replaces X's two look-up items in the 4-5 inverse problem with lists that need real construction. The organizer would spend less of his fifteen minutes per band fixing Y.
